text: John Haberle kept painting paper money despite warnings from the Secret Service. His still lifes of ordinary objects look so real that a viewer can mistake the painting for the objects. He was born in New Haven, the son of Swabian immigrants, and left school at 14 to apprentice with an engraver. For many years he also worked as an illustrator and exhibit preparator for a museum. He is counted as one of three major trompe-l'œil painters in the United States in the late 19th century, along with William Harnett and John Peto.

Nicolás Megía painted historical costumbrista scenes, and many of them are watercolors. He came from Fuente de Cantos and studied under Domingo Valdivieso and Federico de Madrazo. A stipend let him study abroad. In Rome he worked with Marià Fortuny and at the Accademia Chigi, where the Macchiaioli influenced him. Then he went to Paris and worked with Jean-Louis-Ernest Meissonier until 1880.

Paolo Posi studied at the Accademia di San Luca in Rome and, from 1751, served as the family architect of the Colonna. He completed the restoration of the Palazzo Colonna, which Nicola Michetti and Gaetano Chiaveri had started in 1731. The job made him known more as a designer than as an architect. He designed mausoleums for Cardinal Innico Caracciolo in Aversa and for Princess Maria Flaminia Chigi-Odescalchi in Santa Maria del Popolo. He was born in Siena.

Peter Strudel came from Cles in Trentino and went to the Hofburg in Vienna with his brother Paul, who also became a painter to the Imperial Court. He built the Strudelhof mansion in the suburbs and founded a private art school there. It was the first general training center for artists outside the painters' guild, modeled on the Accademia di San Luca and the French Académie Royale. His work marks the transition of Austria to the high baroque style. He was a sculptor as well as a painter.

Vincenzo Campi came from a family of artists in Cremona. His father Galeazzo was a painter, and so were his older brothers Giulio and Antonio. He is thought to have trained in Giulio's workshop. The first record of his work is a portrait, now lost, of Archduke Ernest and his brother Rudolf, painted in 1563 while they stayed in Cremona. He was one of the first artists in northern Italy to work in the Flemish style of realist genre painting. He died in 1591.

Almost nothing is known about Baccio Baldini except that he was buried in Florence in 1487. Vasari says he was a goldsmith and a pupil of Maso Finiguerra, and that he based all his works on designs by Sandro Botticelli because he lacked disegno himself. Today he is best remembered for the first printed Dante in 1481, where the painter probably supplied drawings that Baldini turned into engravings. It does not seem that all his work was Botticelli's. Vasari also claimed, incorrectly, that Finiguerra invented engraving.

Albert Berghaus drew for Frank Leslie's Weekly, making sketches and wood engravings of important events in American history. After the Civil War he traveled in the west. In the late 1870s he worked with Frederic Remington to illustrate Tenting on the Plains, an account by Mrs. George Custer. Original works by Berghaus are extremely scarce. The Smithsonian, the Library of Congress and the White House hold some.

Claude-Guy Hallé won the Prix de Rome in 1675 with Adam's Transgression. His father, Daniel Hallé, was a painter from Rouen. In 1699 he joined the Académie royale with The Restoration of the Catholic Religion in Strasbourg. When the director Louis de Boullogne died in 1733, Hyacinthe Rigaud proposed that the four rectors, Hallé, Nicolas de Largillière, Guillaume Coustou and Rigaud himself, rotate the post. That arrangement lasted until Coustou was elected sole director.

Constantino Brumidi is best known for the fresco Apotheosis of Washington in the Capitol Building. His father was a Greek from Filiatra and his mother was Italian. He trained under Bertel Thorvaldsen, Antonio Canova and Vincenzo Camuccini. He painted in several Roman palaces, among them that of Prince Torlonia. Under Gregory XVI he worked for three years in the Vatican. He later became an American citizen.

David Widhopff was active in the Paris art scene for more than four decades, with Alfons Mucha and the writer Léon Deschamps among his friends. He became a naturalized French citizen. He showed paintings at the Paris Salons in 1888, 1891 and 1893. At the request of the Brazilian government, he later founded a fine-arts academy in the Amazonian state of Pará. There he held several one-man shows and acted as artistic director for several newspapers. He also made caricatures and posters.

Édouard De Bièfve came from a noble family in Brussels and studied at the academy there. From 1828 to 1830 he worked in the school of Joseph Paelinck, a former pupil of Jacques-Louis David. In Paris in 1831 he became a follower of the new romantic movement and went to the studio of the sculptor David d'Angers. He sculpted and painted at the same time. He was one of the leading representatives of the romantic movement in Belgium, and his work influenced history painting in Germany.

Francescuccio Ghissi, also called Francesco di Cecco Ghissi, is known to have worked with Allegretto Nuzi. His exact dates of birth and death are not known, but he was active from 1359 to 1395. He painted mostly religious works for church commissions in the Marche region. Little is known about his activities beyond a Madonna of Humility, part of a triptych now at Polesden Lacey in the National Trust collection. He also has works in the Pinacoteca Civica of Fabriano and painted for the Cathedral of Fabriano.

Friedrich Fehr studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich with Alexander Strähuber, Gyula Benczúr and Ludwig von Löfftz. A scholarship from the Martin von Wagner Foundation then paid for a long study trip to Italy. On his return to Munich he founded a private art school with Ludwig Schmid-Reutte. Its students included Emil Nolde and Clara Rilke-Westhoff. His father, Kaspar Fehr, was a notary in Werneck. He painted in the Historicist style.

Giovanni da Udine's real name was Giovanni Nanni. He worked as a student and assistant of Raphael and was responsible for most of the decorative, non-narrative parts of Raphael's big projects in Rome. He specialised in fresco and stucco grotesques. His stucco work is in the Loggia di Raffaello at the Vatican, and his heavy fruit-laden wreaths are in the Loggia of Psyche at the Villa Farnesina. He also helped build a few monumental fountains, now destroyed. He is also known for his drawings of birds and fruit.

Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi ran the most important printing press in 17th-century Rome. His father, Giuseppe de Rossi, founded it, and after Giuseppe died it passed to Giovanni Giacomo and his brother Giandomenico. Of the family members who ran the press, Giovanni Giacomo was the most involved, and he took the company to the height of its success. He printed etchings for artists including Giovanni Benedetto Castiglione and Pietro Testa. He was active in Rome from 1648 to 1691.

Hans Ulrich Franck came from Kaufbeuren in Swabia and lived mostly in Augsburg, where he died in 1675. He painted historical subjects and also etched. One of his series is twenty-five plates of scenes from military life, dated 1656. Other etchings show the meeting of David and Abigail and Alexander with the dying Darius. His son Franz Friedrich Franck was an artist as well.

Ilya Chashnik was eleven when he started at Yehuda Pen's art school in Vitebsk. He later became a student of Marc Chagall. By 1918 he had moved to Moscow to work in a workshop directed by Kazimir Malevich, and he returned to Vitebsk after Malevich took a senior teaching position there. He became a pupil of Malevich and a founding member of the UNOVIS school. He was able in a variety of media. He died in 1929, at 26.

João Marques de Oliveira entered the academy in Porto at eleven. He graduated in 1873 and then lived for six years in France with his colleague António da Silva Porto. The two studied at the École des Beaux-Arts under Alexandre Cabanel and Adolphe Yvon. They also made study trips to Belgium, England, the Netherlands and Italy, and the sketches and paintings from those trips led to his participation in the Salons of 1876. Then he went home. He worked as a free-lance artist.

Daniel Havell's uncle was the engraver Robert Havell the Elder. Daniel moved to London and set up as an aquatint engraver in partnership with Robert Havell. Together they published Twenty Four Views Taken in St. Helena, after pictures by Henry Salt. The partnership did not last, and Daniel worked on his own, making plates for Ackermann's History of Cambridge and a celebrated view of St Paul's Cathedral. His last work was a book on the theatres of London, published in 1826. He was buried in Kingston upon Thames in 1822.

Juriaen van Streeck painted still lifes, and according to Houbraken he excelled at every subject, from helmets and books to skulls and dead animals that point to the transience of life. He followed Willem Kalf and influenced Barend van der Meer. He married Grietje Claes in 1653, and they had nine children, three of whom were buried young. The family lived in the Jordaan and then on the Prinsengracht. When he died he was an innkeeper in Kerkstraat.

Kanō Masanobu was the chief painter of the Ashikaga shogunate and is generally considered the founder of the Kanō school. His father, Kanō Kagenobu, was a samurai and amateur artist, but Masanobu started the line of professional artists in the family. He was influenced by the priest-painter Tenshō Shūbun. He worked in the suiboku ink and wash style, which comes from Chinese painting, but gave it a Japanese touch with more defined forms. He specialized in Zen paintings and in elaborate paintings of Buddhist deities.

Ludvig Munthe grew up near Sogndalsfjøra in Norway and came to Bergen in 1858, where the German painter and architect Franz Wilhelm Schiertz taught him first. He then moved to Düsseldorf, became a pupil of Albert Flamm at the Kunstakademie and stayed in the city for good. His paintings treat their subjects realistically. He liked autumn and winter scenes in stormy or gloomy weather, as well as forest and coast views. He belonged to the Düsseldorf school.

Manuel García took the name Hispaleto from his older brother Rafael, who had adopted it as a pseudonym in 1853. It comes from Hispalis, the Roman name of Seville. After Rafael died at twenty-two, Manuel began using it himself. He was born in Seville, where his father ran a moderately successful import business. In 1847, at eleven, he began classes at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de Santa Isabel de Hungría. He painted portraits and costumbrista scenes.

Nicolaas de Liemaker, also called Nicolaes Roose, was the son of a glass painter in Ghent. Descamps says he studied with Markus Geeraerts the younger, but that is unlikely, and he probably studied under Otto van Veen in Antwerp instead. In 1625 he returned to Ghent, where he died in 1646. The museum of Ghent and the churches of the city and of other Flemish towns own many of his works. His Consecration of St. Nicholas, Bishop of Myra, above the high altar of the church of St. Nicholas, is considered his best picture.

Paul Mathey was the son of a restorer in Paris. He learned his art at the École des Beaux-Arts under Léon Cogniet and others. He began to exhibit at the Salon in 1868 and became a recognized portrait painter. He often portrayed artists from his circle in their studios. He also painted landscapes, seascapes and decorations. At forty-four he took up engraving.

Pierre-Jean David took the name David d'Angers when he entered the studio of the painter Jacques-Louis David in 1809, to show where he came from and to tell himself apart from the master. His father was a wood carver and ornamental sculptor who fought as a musketeer in the Republican army against the Chouans of La Vendée. David studied with Jean-Jacques Delusse and in 1808 went to Paris, to the studio of Philippe-Laurent Roland. There he worked on the Arc de Triomphe and the exterior of the Louvre. He was also a medalist and an active freemason.

Pieter de Putter was among the first generation of artists who specialised in fish still lifes. He mainly painted fish, game pieces and still lifes with figures. He was born in Middelburg around 1600, the son of the painter Joost de Putter, of whom no surviving works are known. The family lived in The Hague from 1605, and his father gave him his first training. In 1626 he married Maria van den Queborn. She was the aunt of Anna van den Queborn, who married the painter Abraham van Beijeren.
